lesson.title: Class Methods: Behavior That Belongs to the Class Itself
lesson.summary: A class method, marked with @classmethod, receives the class itself as cls instead of receiving an individual instance as self, which makes it the right tool for working with class-level data shared by every object and for building alternative ways to construct an object.
lesson.body:
Every method you've written so far has been an instance method: called on one specific object, receiving that object as self, and typically working with that object's own attributes. But some things a class needs to do aren't really about any one object, they're about the class as a whole. Recall class attributes, a piece of data that lives on the class itself and is shared by every instance rather than duplicated on each one. Working with that kind of shared data is exactly what a class method is for.

You mark a method as a class method with the @classmethod decorator placed directly above its definition, and its first parameter is named cls instead of self, by convention, referring to the class itself rather than to any particular instance. When you call a class method, Python automatically supplies the class as that first argument, the same automatic behavior you already know from self, just one level up, bound to the class instead of to an object.

```python
class Robot:
    population = 0

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        Robot.population += 1

    @classmethod
    def from_default_name(cls, number):
        return cls(f"Robot-{number}")

    @classmethod
    def get_population(cls):
        return cls.population

r1 = Robot("WALL-E")
r2 = Robot.from_default_name(2)

print(r1.name)
# Output: WALL-E
print(r2.name)
# Output: Robot-2
print(Robot.get_population())
# Output: 2
```

Trace it carefully. population is a class attribute, starting at 0, shared by the whole Robot class rather than owned separately by each robot. r1 = Robot("WALL-E") runs __init__, sets self.name to "WALL-E", and increments Robot.population to 1. Then r2 = Robot.from_default_name(2) calls the class method with cls bound to Robot; inside it, cls(f"Robot-{number}") builds the string "Robot-2" and calls Robot("Robot-2"), which runs __init__ again, setting self.name to "Robot-2" and bumping Robot.population to 2. print(r1.name) shows WALL-E, print(r2.name) shows Robot-2, and Robot.get_population(), another class method, returns cls.population, which is 2.

Two things stand out here. First, from_default_name is an alternative constructor: it offers a second, named way to build a Robot (with a default, numbered name) without changing what __init__ itself requires. Second, get_population works with data that belongs to the class, not to r1 or r2 individually, so it makes far more sense as a class method than as an instance method that happens to ignore self. Whenever a method's job is about the class as a whole, shared counters, alternative ways to build objects, class-wide configuration, reach for @classmethod and cls instead of an ordinary instance method.
